translator: Claude (AI), draft, not reviewed by a Hittitologist
intro: This tablet is an anthology of three rituals against epidemic, copied one after another: the ritual of Zarpiya, physician of Kizzuwatna (§1–19), the ritual of Uḫḫamuwa of Arzawa (§20–23) and the ritual of Ašḫella of Ḫapalla (§24–29), with a closing colophon (§30). The same three rituals, in the same order, stand on KUB 9.31.

sections.title: Ritual of Zarpiya, physician of Kizzuwatna
Ritual of Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa
Ritual of Ašḫella, man of Ḫapalla

paras.en: [… he han]gs [up …]
[… r]ed [wool] … [… o]pposite … On one side […] [and on the other si]de, in a peg of cornel(?) wood […]

[… in fr]ont, in the gate, a peg of medlar(?) wood […]. Then of barley flour […] [cook]ed and … […] he hangs up a jug of wine. […] he strikes the cornel(?) wood. […] a cooked kukkulla-(cake) […] a kukkulla-(cake) and one jug of wine he h[angs up].

[…] … a ḫaḫḫal-branch he sticks in, and below […] below, in front, […] on this side … its name (is) ḫuwallari (?). Then in whichever gate (the ritual) is (held), he hangs the kelamuš (?) behind the door of the courtyard. Below, in front, he sets up one wicker table for the kelawa-(ritual). On it he places a bronze axe, one warm loaf, one thick loaf and cheese; and on top he places a bronze axe, a bronze dagger, a drawn bronze bow and an arrow.
Below, in front of the table, he places one bowl of wine on a tray and one jug of (beer-)drink on a tray, and into the jug of drink he sets one drinking straw.

They drive up one billy goat, and the master of the house offers it with wine to Šanta before the table. He holds out the bronze axe and speaks thus: 'Come, Šanta! With you let the Innarawant-gods come, who are clothed in bloody (garments), who have the ḫupru- of the lulaḫi-men bound on,

who are girded with daggers, who have their bows drawn and hold arrows! Come and eat!' When he has finished speaking the oath(?), he sets the bronze axe down on the table, and they stab the billy goat.

He takes the blood and smears it on the drinking straw that has been set in the jug of drink. They bring the liver and the heart raw, and he holds them out to the master of the house (and) to the god. Then they make an imitation of biting (them), put a lip to the drinking straw, and he sips, and speaks thus:
'Here, Šanta and Innarawant-gods, we have sworn an oath!

We have bitten from the raw liver, and we have drunk from one straw. So, Šanta and Innarawant-gods, do not step to my gate again!' And they cook the liver and heart in the fire, and they cut up the whole billy goat plainly.

When the fat is done, they bring the liver, the heart and all the meat forth to the god. Beside it they bring twice nine thick loaves of emmer flour, (each of) half a handful. He breaks the nine thick loaves; on them they put the liver and the heart, and he sets it back on the table and speaks thus: 'Above and below, Sun-god of Heaven, eat! Let the father-gods of the house eat! Let the Thousand Gods eat!
And be witnesses to this oath!' Afterwards he libates wine nine times before the table of the Innarawant-gods, places the shoulder and the breast on it, and breaks the nine thick loaves.
[Luwian incantation, only partly understood: '… the foot(?) … evil … sheep, cattle, human beings … do not eat(?) …']
He breaks a thick loaf and then [speaks] in Lu[wian]:
[Luwian incantation, not securely understood: 'O great(?) Sun-god, father-gods, … into the house(?) … as they take(?) …']
[Luwian line naming the god A.A (Aya?), not understood.]
They take up the ritual implements; he closes the door, anoints it with fine oil and speaks:
'Let evil be shut out(?); let good be held fast(?) inside!'
One long tablet, complete: the word of Zarpiya, physician of the land of Kizzuwatna. If the year is bad and there is continual dying in the land, he performs the kilawa-ritual as follows.
Thus (says) Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa: If there is continual dying in the land, and if some enemy god has caused it, then I do as follows:

They drive up one ram. They twist together blue wool, red wool, yellow wool, black wool and white wool and make it into a crown, and they crown the ram. They drive the ram out onto the road of the enemy, and while doing so they speak thus: 'Whatever god of the enemy land has caused this plague — see, we have driven this crowned ram to you, the god, for peace. Just as a … is firm(?), be at peace with this ram! And you, whatever god has caused this death, make peace in the same way with the land of Ḫattuša, and turn again in favour towards the land of Ḫattuša!' And they drive the one crowned ram away into the enemy land.

Afterwards they bring fodder and tallow for the god's horses, and they speak thus: 'You have harnessed the horses: let them eat this fodder and be sated. Let your chariot be greased with tallow. O god, Storm-god, turn back to your own land, but turn in favour towards the land of Ḫattuša!'

Afterwards one billy goat (and) two sheep are killed(?): he offers the billy goat to the Sebettu (the 'Seven'), and one sheep they kill and cook. Then they bring one cheese, one sour (loaf), one pulla-vessel of sour bread, one bowl of wine, one bowl of beer and fruit, and they prepare them for the god of the road.

Thus (says) [Ašḫel]la, man of Ḫapalla: If in the land or in the army camp there is dying, then I perform this ritual. I take these things: when evening comes on the day, whoever are the lords of the army, each prepares a ram — whether they are light or dark does not matter at all. And I twist together a cord of white wool, red wool and green wool, and he weaves it into one; I set into it one bead and one ring of lead, and I bind it on the necks and horns of the rams. At night they tie them up in front of the tents, and while doing so they speak thus: 'Whatever god is roaming about, whatever god has caused this plague — see, I have tied up these rams for you: be appeased by them!'

In the morning I drive them to the open country. And with each ram they bring one jug, one thick loaf and one cup. In front of the king's tent they seat a decorated woman, and he places a bowl of beer and three thick loaves beside the woman.

Then the lords of the army place their hands on the rams, and they speak thus: 'Whatever god has caused this plague, see, the rams now stand (here), and they are very fat in liver, heart and loins. Let human flesh be hateful to him; be appeased by these rams!' The lords of the army bow down behind the rams, and the king bows down behind the decorated woman. Then they carry the rams, the woman, the bread and the beer out through the middle of the army and drive them to the open country. They go and let them run off into the enemy's border(-land), [to a pla]ce where none of us goes, (saying): 'See, […]' [— a few lines are lost; the second piece mentions fourteen thick loaves, driving them to the open country, ‘all this’, branches and fat —] '[…] with the god's (portion) cooked; then with meat, bread and beer we have given (you) […]. O god, eat and drink in a godly way, but hand nothing over to mankind(?)!' They bow down behind them, and they come away. While they are appeasing the god, no one sets any implement down on the ground; and it is not permitted to pick it up again.

When they come away from the ritual, they pour salt into water and wash their hands with it. Then they kindle fire in two places and walk out between them. In front(?) he prepares two billy goats, one bowl of wine and five thick loaves, and he offers the two billy goats to the Tutelary Deity of the (field) equipment(?). He places the breast, the right shoulder, the liver and the heart, cooked, on leafy branches, and drinks three times to the Tutelary Deity of the (field) equipment(?). They eat, and come away.

On the third day, when it grows light in the early morning, they quickly drive up one billy goat, one sheep and one pig, and behind them they prepare three thick loaves and one bowl of beer. They drive them to the open country, to another place. They spread out leafy branches and set the three thick loaves back (on them), and they offer the billy goat, the sheep and the pig to that god (saying): 'Whatever god has caused this plague in the army camp, let that god eat and drink, and let him be at peace with the land of Ḫattuša and with the army of Ḫattuša, and let him turn inward in favour!' They eat and drink, and come away.

On the fourth day, when it grows light in the early morning, they quickly drive up one bull, one ewe and three sheep — a ewe to which a ram has not yet gone — with ten thick loaves, one bowl of beer and one bowl of wine, and they drive them to the open country, to another place. They offer the bull to the Storm-god, the ewe to the Sun-god, and the three sheep to all the gods. They spread leafy branches on the ground and set back (on them) the breast, the right shoulder, the liver, the heart and the thick loaves, cooked; and they drink three times to the Sun-god of Heaven, the Storm-god and all the gods. They eat, and come away.
[Colophon:] […] three rituals are set down (on this tablet): […] in the army camp.
